newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil pensions minister sees pitfalls for reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil pensions minister sees pitfalls for reform.

text.p: Brazilian Social Security Minister Reinhold Stephanes said Tuesday a new version of the government's pension reform bill might not be approved before next year's elections.

"If the reform is not approved this year then it will have to be done in the future," Stephanes said in an interview with national CBN Radio. "Otherwise we'll be left high and dry by our own (growth) dynamics."

Senator Benavides Veras was due to present a new version of the reform bill to a Senate committee Tuesday. The bill has been rewritten to include several key points which were defeated during voting in the Chamber of Deputies last year.
Stephanes said he expected a smooth passage for the reform in the Senate but more difficulties when it returns to the lower house for approval of the changes.
The Chamber of Deputies has grown steadily less responsive to the government's reform program as next year's elections loom and lawmakers worry about their standing in the eyes of the electorate.
Government officials have said they believe September will prove the cut-off point for the reforms in Congress, ahead of the October 1998 presidential and congressional elections.
As a constitutional amendment, the pension reform bill needs two three-fifths majorities on the floor of both houses.

The bill seeks to plug a growing social security deficit, expected to reach $2 billion in 1997, via a series of measures including the introduction of minimum retirement ages and tying pensions to contributions paid rather than time served.

Stephanes said the legislation would bring Brazil's social security system in line with those of other Latin American countries and would prevent abnormalities such as professionals receiving pensions from as young as 35.
"We should have done this reform ten years ago," he said.
